lede: A body that is not accelerating has forces that cancel exactly. That single idea turns a picture of four forces into two ordinary equations, and those equations are where most of the marks in a Unit 2 forces question live.
can: Recognise when a body is in equilibrium and say what that means for its forces
Write two component equations, with every force in each of them
Solve for an unknown force or angle, on the flat and on a slope

md: Stand still and two forces act on you: the Earth pulls you down, the floor pushes you up, and they match. Hang a picture and three forces settle into the same kind of balance. Nothing is moving, so nothing is left over.

alt: A particle at O held still by three forces: 20 N horizontally to the right, 15 N vertically downwards, and 25 N up and to the left at 36.87 degrees to the horizontal.

caption: Three forces that add to nothing at all.

md:
A particle is in equilibrium when the resultant of the forces on it is zero. Not small: zero. The single force that would replace them all does not exist, because they already cancel.

That is why a body in equilibrium either stays still or keeps moving at a steady speed in a straight line. There is nothing left over to change its motion.

prompt: A particle is in equilibrium under three forces. What is the resultant of those forces?
options: the sum of the three sizes
explain: If anything were left over the particle would accelerate. Equilibrium is exactly the case where nothing is.

alt: A five-row table of the method: draw every force with a label, choose two perpendicular directions, resolve each force into those directions, set the total in each direction to zero, then solve the pair of equations.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 471 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='471' height='240'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><rect x='2' y='2' width='467' height='236' rx='8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1' stroke-opacity='0.5'/><text x='12' y='35' text-anchor='start' font-size='13.5' font-weight='600'>Solving an equilibrium problem</text><text x='12' y='65' text-anchor='start' font-size='12' font-weight='600'>Step</text><text x='152' y='65' text-anchor='start' font-size='12' font-weight='600'>What you write</text><text x='12' y='95' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>draw</text><text x='152' y='95' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>every force on the body, with a label</text><text x='12' y='125' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>choose</text><text x='152' y='125' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>two perpendicular directions</text><text x='12' y='155' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>resolve</text><text x='152' y='155' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>each force into those two directions</text><text x='12' y='185' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>equate</text><text x='152' y='185' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>the total in each direction to zero</text><text x='12' y='215' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>solve</text><text x='152' y='215' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>the pair of equations for the unknowns</text><path d='M6 76H465M6 106H465M6 136H465M6 166H465M6 196H465M6 226H465M146 46V226' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='0.8' stroke-opacity='0.45'/></g></svg>
caption: The same five lines every time.

md:
A zero resultant means zero in every direction, so choose two perpendicular ones and write an equation for each. Horizontal and vertical on the flat; along the slope and at right angles to it on a slope.

Two equations are what let you find two unknowns. One component written down on its own earns a method mark at best: the marks after that are for the equation.

title: Why two directions are enough
md: Any force can be rebuilt from its parts along two perpendicular directions, so if both totals are zero there is nothing left in any direction at all. A third equation would only repeat what the first two already say.

prompt: A candidate resolves one force on a body in equilibrium and writes down its vertical component, then stops. What is missing?
options: an equation setting the total of every vertical force to zero
the horizontal component of that same force
answer: an equation setting the total of every vertical force to zero
explain: A single component is the start of the method. The marks that follow are for putting every vertical force into one equation.

text: 3. Every force goes into the equation

caption: Four forces, and all four appear in one line each.

md:
The commonest way marks go is an equation with too few terms. Here the block is held by a rope at $50°$, so the vertical equation has three forces in it, not two.

Resolving vertically: $R + 24\sin 50° = 60$, so $R = 41.61$ N. Writing $R = 60$ ignores the rope's lift; writing $R = 24\sin 50°$ ignores the weight.

title: What the reports keep saying
md: Equations with only two terms are described as very common, and a large number of candidates never set up the vertical equation at all. Both lose the marks that the equation itself carries.

prompt: A block of weight 60 N rests on a table and a rope pulls it with a vertical component of 24 N upwards. What is the normal reaction, in newtons?
explain: Resolving vertically, $R + 24 = 60$, so $R = 36$ N. The rope takes part of the weight, so the table supports less.

text: 4. On a slope, resolve along and across it

alt: A box of mass 14 kg held at rest on a smooth slope inclined at 27 degrees. R leaves the box at right angles to the slope, 140 N points straight down, and T points up the slope along a rope.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 364 264' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='364' height='264'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M45.8 198.8L330.9 53.6L330.9 198.8Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M57.8 207.8l8 -9M73.8 207.8l8 -9M89.8 207.8l8 -9M105.8 207.8l8 -9M121.8 207.8l8 -9M137.8 207.8l8 -9M153.8 207.8l8 -9M169.8 207.8l8 -9M185.8 207.8l8 -9M201.8 207.8l8 -9M217.8 207.8l8 -9M233.8 207.8l8 -9M249.8 207.8l8 -9M265.8 207.8l8 -9M281.8 207.8l8 -9M297.8 207.8l8 -9M313.8 207.8l8 -9' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='0.8' stroke-opacity='0.45'/><path d='M79.8 198.8A34 34 0 0 0 76.1 183.4' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='87.8' y='189.8' text-anchor='start' font-size='12'>27°</text><text x='330.9' y='220.8' text-anchor='end' font-size='11.5'>smooth slope</text><path d='M182.7 90.9L234.4 64.6L249.8 94.9L198.2 121.2Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='216.3' y='96.9' text-anchor='middle' font-size='12'>14 kg</text><path d='M208.6 77.7L187.2 35.9' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.9' stroke-opacity='1'/><path d='M187.2 35.9L194.7 42.2L187.9 45.6Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='184' y='24.6' text-anchor='end' font-size='12.5' font-weight='600'>R</text><path d='M216.3 112L216.3 168.9' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.9' stroke-opacity='1'/><path d='M216.3 168.9L212.5 159.9L220.1 159.9Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='216.3' y='187.9' text-anchor='start' font-size='12.5' font-weight='600'>140 N</text><path d='M242.1 79.7L273.3 63.8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.9' stroke-opacity='1'/><path d='M273.3 63.8L267 71.3L263.6 64.5Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='279.5' y='55.7' text-anchor='start' font-size='12.5' font-weight='600'>T</text></g></svg>
caption: Along the slope and at right angles to it.

md:
On a slope the useful pair of directions is along the surface and perpendicular to it, because two of the three forces already lie along them.

Only the weight has to be resolved. Along the slope: $T = 140\sin 27° = 63.56$ N. At right angles: $R = 140\cos 27° = 124.74$ N. The reaction is less than the weight here: only $140\cos 27°$ presses into the slope, and $\cos 27°$ is less than 1.

prompt: A box is held at rest on a smooth slope by a rope parallel to the slope. How does the normal reaction on it compare with its weight?
options: it is smaller than the weight
it is equal to the weight
it is larger than the weight
answer: it is smaller than the weight
explain: Only the part of the weight pressing into the surface has to be balanced, and $\cos\alpha$ is less than one for any real slope.

text: 5. A rough slope holding a body still

alt: A crate of mass 7 kg at rest on a rough slope inclined at 18 degrees, with nothing attached to it. R leaves the crate at right angles to the slope, 70 N points straight down, and F acts up the slope.

caption: No rope: friction is what holds it.

md:
Take the rope away and a box on a rough slope can still sit there. Friction has taken the rope's place, so it acts up the slope and matches the component of the weight pulling the box down it.

For a $7$ kg crate on an $18°$ slope: $F = 70\sin 18° = 21.63$ N up the slope, and $R = 70\cos 18° = 66.57$ N.

prompt: A crate rests on a rough slope with nothing attached to it. Which force balances the component of the weight acting down the slope?
options: the force due to friction, acting up the slope
answer: the force due to friction, acting up the slope
explain: The reaction is at right angles to the slope, so it can do nothing along it. Friction is the only force left that lies along the surface.

alt: A table matching four descriptions to their meaning. At rest, held still, and moving at constant velocity all mean the forces balance. Speeding up or slowing down means they do not, and Newton's Second Law is used instead.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 442 210' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='442' height='210'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><rect x='2' y='2' width='438' height='206' rx='8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1' stroke-opacity='0.5'/><text x='12' y='35' text-anchor='start' font-size='13.5' font-weight='600'>When a body is in equilibrium</text><text x='12' y='65' text-anchor='start' font-size='12' font-weight='600'>What the question says</text><text x='236' y='65' text-anchor='start' font-size='12' font-weight='600'>What it means</text><text x='12' y='95' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>at rest</text><text x='236' y='95' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>the forces balance</text><text x='12' y='125' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>held still</text><text x='236' y='125' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>the forces balance</text><text x='12' y='155' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>moving at constant velocity</text><text x='236' y='155' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>the forces balance</text><text x='12' y='185' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>speeding up or slowing down</text><text x='236' y='185' text-anchor='start' font-size='13'>they do not: use F = ma</text><path d='M6 76H436M6 106H436M6 136H436M6 166H436M6 196H436M230 46V196' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='0.8' stroke-opacity='0.45'/></g></svg>
caption: Four phrases, and what each one is telling you.

md:
Equilibrium does not mean stationary. A body moving at constant velocity is not accelerating, so $F = ma$ gives $F = 0$ and the forces balance exactly as they do at rest.

So *at rest*, *held still* and *moving with constant velocity* are all the same instruction: write two equations, each equal to zero.

title: FM Mechanics resolving around a point
why: Taught straight against this specification. Watch the two directions being named in writing before either equation is formed.

prompt: A crate is being dragged across a floor at a constant velocity of 2 m/s. What is true of the forces on it?
options: they balance, because the acceleration is zero
they do not balance, because it is moving
the driving force must be the largest
answer: they balance, because the acceleration is zero
explain: Constant velocity means no acceleration, and $F = ma$ with $a = 0$ makes the resultant zero. Motion at a steady speed needs no force left over.

md:
Say what equilibrium means and recognise it from at rest, held still or constant velocity.
Choose two perpendicular directions and write a complete equation for each.
Put every force into every equation, including the ones that have to be resolved.
Solve for an unknown force or angle on the flat and on a slope.
Use friction as the force that holds a body still on a rough slope.

An equilibrium part is worth 2 or 3 marks and is worded 'Calculate the value of' or 'Calculate the normal reaction'. The first mark is for naming the direction you are resolving in and writing a complete equation; the last is for the value to 2 decimal places. Stuck? Write 'resolving vertically' on its own line, then list every force that has a vertical part.
